title: Signal isolation workflow & quick-reference
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a compact, pragmatic workflow for isolating performance regressions when a production alert or a canary delta is detected. It focuses on signal enrichment, lightweight repro, targeted profiling, and a fast commit-level isolation path. Use this as a checklist during the first 4 hours of an investigation: quick, reversible, and oriented toward returning the fleet to signal baseline.

Context notes:
- We care about token tail latency and 95/99/99.9p shifts, but often the root cause is outside the model kernels: scheduler path, KV cache, request batching, routing policy, or runtime kernel selection.
- This flow assumes you have dashboard-level evidence (time range, cluster, model id, route) and a few example request IDs or traces.

1) Initial triage (15–30m) — signal framing
- Collect: alert ID, time window, affected clusters/regions, model variant, canary vs prod, approximate token lengths, and sample request IDs.
- Snapshot dashboards: export panels for 10m before and 30m after alert. Keep CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, scheduling latency, disk I/O, network retransmits, and token-per-second metrics.
- Decide whether to immediately rollback canary or continue investigation in place. If customer-facing SLA is at risk, rollback first; if metric delta < configured escalation and we can maintain capacity, proceed.

2) Quick enrichment (30–60m) — attach context
- Pull traces for 10–20 impacted requests. Prioritize requests with long tail tokens.
- Enrich with metadata: request size, route config, batching group id, whether prefix cache hit occurred, and the environment (host kernel driver versions, CUDA runtime, container image hash).
- Add an ephemeral Grafana overlay that shows per-instance 95/99p and request counts (toggle by host). This often surfaces whether the regression is limited to a small subset of hosts.

3) Narrow the subset (30–60m) — host/cluster isolation
- If only a few hosts show anomalies, isolate them via Canary-Pool tagging and drain new traffic. Collect full runtime dumps from one problematic host (see dump checklist).
- If the anomaly is fleet-wide, split by model variant, CPU/GPU type, and routing tier to find correlated dimensions.

Dump checklist (what to collect from a host)
- Kernel traces: perf record top-down for 60s during reproduction.
- Runtime logs: serving-runtime.log (last 2k lines) + model-server stdout.
- KV cache metrics: hit/miss rate, eviction rate, cache warmup time for that model version.
- Batching telemetry: average batch size, batch wait time histogram, and continuous-batching config snapshot.
- Environment: container image hash, driver versions (NVIDIA/CUDA), kernel version, nvidia-smi output, and any installed microcode/firmware version notes.

4) Lightweight repro & synthetic smoke (45–90m)
- Reproduce a minimal repro: re-run 1–5 example requests on an isolated canary cluster with exact headers/route and single-host configuration. If regression reproduces, increase concurrency slowly to map the throughput/latency surface.
- If repro does not reproduce, try to replay the live trace through the local executor (we have a trace-replay tool: scripts/trace_replay.py) to verify whether the issue depends on real network/queue shapes.

5) Targeted profiling (1–2h) — where to look first
- Token path hotspot: sample token latency by token index (prefix vs continuation). If later tokens are slower, suspect KV cache or attention cache eviction.
- Scheduler and batching hotpath: instrument scheduler queue time and per-request stall events. A sudden jump in per-request schedule latency often points to adaptive-batch tuning or a GC/locking regresson in the request queue.
- GPU kernel skew: compare kernel launch and sync times across hosts. Wide variance + identical model weights implies driver or contention.
- Small-call overheads: measure the percent of time spent in framework overhead (marshalling, quantization conversion) vs kernel execution.

Commands / snippets to run during profiling (quick paste)
- perf top/capture: perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60; perf script | flamegraph.pl > out.svg
- nvprof-like quick check: nsys profile --output host_trace --capture-range cstart:1 --duration 60s <serving-binary>
- collect logs: tar czf host-dump-<host>-<ts>.tgz /var/log/serving/*.log /opt/model-caches/* /tmp/kvmetrics.json

6) Commit-level isolation (2–6h) — fast bisect approach
- Preconditions: you need a deterministic synthetic repro and a narrow commit window (last rolling release or infra image bump).
- If infra image changed recently: isolate by re-deploying prior image to a small canary subset and compare.
- Git-level bisect (when code suspected): use our accelerated bisect harness which runs a minimal smoke test that mimics the problematic request class. Command: scripts/fast_bisect.sh --start <bad_sha> --end <good_sha> --smoke tests/perf/smoke_token_tail.py
- If a config or flag flip is suspected, use config-rollout to toggle the flag in a canary and re-check panels.

7) Canary comparison checklist (post-rollout or against control)
- Panels to compare side-by-side: p99 latency by token index, scheduler queue latency, batch size distribution, GPU utilization percentiles, KV hit rate, cross-host latency variance.
- Look for asymmetric patterns: e.g., canary has identical mean latency but heavier right tail and higher variance across hosts. That suggests increased non-deterministic stalls rather than systematic kernel slowdown.

Hypotheses that often hold true (and what to test)
- Kernel regression: reproduce offline on same driver + container baseline; if reproduces, record exact kernel names and call stacks.
- CVM/driver interactions: compare nvidia-smi and driver versions; many tail regressions follow minor driver updates.
- Adaptive batching misconfiguration: temporarily fix batch size cap and observe tail recovery.
- KV cache poisoning: debug by forcing cold cache and measuring warmup curve; correlate with recent rollout that changed cache keying.

Postmortem quick structure (to fill within 24–48h)
- Summary: what changed, impact numbers (tokens/sec, p99 uplift, customer impact), scope (hosts/users/routes).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence: clear bullets mapping evidence to claims (dashboards, flamegraphs, traces, repro).
- Fix implemented: code/config rollback, kernel patch, driver pin, or further tracking.
- Follow-ups: instrumentation gaps, monitoring additions, gating for future rollout, and owners.

Notes and heuristics (ops experience)
- Don’t trust single-run profiles. Take 3–5 profiles spaced 5–10 minutes apart to rule out transient noise (GC, OS background tasks).
- Token-length quartiles: always analyze separately. A regression that affects only long sequences is usually end-to-end scheduling or kernel memory-path related.
- Small host population anomalies are more likely infra (node-level), while gradual fleet-wide increases after a deploy point to code/config.

Appendix: quick triage decision tree (one-line)
- Is the regression limited to <5% of hosts? -> collect host dumps and isolate host image
- Fleet-wide at deploy time? -> rollback to previous deploy and bisect commits between deploys
- Fleet-wide but no deploy? -> check routing/traffic shape changes, autoscaler policy, and external dependencies

A couple of mental checkboxes to keep stress low:
- Is this customer-impacting right now? If yes, prioritize rollback and mitigation.
- Are we likely to need a long repro? Create a ticket and capture ephemeral artifacts before any rollback.

End of notes.
If useful, I can expand this into a one-page quick reference card or bake the common commands into a runnable incident script. Also flagging follow-ups for improving per-request token-index tracing and making the fast_bisect harness more permissive for infra-image diffs.
